title: Flu Season Starts Early in the U.S.
summary: Flu season has started early in the United States, and it is spreading fast. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday that seven states had high flu activity last week. Louisiana is worst hit so far. Dr. Fred Lopez of New Orleans said flu season is taking off and will likely keep increasing. He urged everyone not yet vaccinated to get vaccinated now. The CDC estimates at least 2.6 million people have fallen ill, with 36,000 hospitalisations and 2,100 deaths. In mid-October, the hospitalisation rate was the highest that early in autumn in more than 15 years, said Dr. Anna Durbin. The surge began in the South and West, including California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington. Doctors expect flu to spread faster as people travel for Thanksgiving. Most illnesses are from a version of H1N1 that may slip past the body's defences, but the vaccine can still work against it, said Andrew Pekosz of Johns Hopkins. Lopez said people should still get a flu shot even if they already caught flu this autumn.
why_it_matters: Getting a flu shot can help protect you and your family from missing school, sports, or holiday time with relatives because of illness.

keywords.explanation: Vaccinated means a person has had a vaccine to help protect against an illness.
Hospitalisations are times when people need to stay in hospital for treatment.
Defences are the ways the body fights off germs and illness.
H1N1 is the name of a type of flu virus.
A surge is a sudden fast rise in something.

background_read: Flu is an illness caused by a virus that spreads from person to person, often through coughs and sneezes.
A flu vaccine teaches the body how to fight the virus, so the illness is usually milder if a person catches it.
Flu spreads more easily when many people travel and gather indoors, which happens around holidays.
